\title{Calibrated Escalation for IT Ticket Triage:\\
What the Calibration Distribution Decides}

\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{TODO author list}
\IEEEauthorblockA{TODO affiliation\\TODO email}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
An IT ticket triage system has to route a ticket to the right team. It also has to recognise when it should not answer at all, and hand the ticket to a person. We build a triage pipeline around that second requirement. It has two independently calibrated escalation gates: a confidence threshold on a lexical first-tier classifier, and a similarity threshold on retrieval. The retrieval gate decides whether a language model may draft a resolution grounded in past tickets. We then test the machinery the way a deployment would stress it. A zero-shot LLM classifies more accurately than our trained classifier, but it has no abstention guarantee, no calibrated gate and no cost model; that contrast is the argument of the paper. Across coverage guarantees, drift monitoring and classification, one result recurs: the data distribution a component is fitted or calibrated on, not the method or the test applied to it, is the binding constraint. We also report what did not work. The two-tier cascade is a latency optimisation, not an accuracy gain. A retrieval-sufficiency check catches both unsupported drafts and is still not usable as a gate. An LLM judge agreed with human labels at a chance-level Cohen's $\kappa$. Every number in this paper is regenerated from a committed result file, and we describe the audit discipline that found and corrected several of our own published figures.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
ticket triage, selective prediction, conformal prediction, retrieval-augmented generation, escalation, reproducibility
\end{IEEEkeywords}

% ===========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% ===========================================================================
Support tickets arrive as free text written by people who do not know which team owns their problem. A triage system that routes a ticket confidently and wrongly costs more than one that asks for help: the ticket waits in the wrong queue, and an automatically drafted fix may be applied to the wrong problem. The design question for such a system is therefore not only how accurate it is, but when it declines to answer.

We treat escalation to a human as the primary output of a triage pipeline rather than an afterthought. Our pipeline classifies a ticket into one of \nb{T19.categories} teams with a two-tier cascade, retrieves similar resolved tickets, and allows a language model to draft a resolution only when retrieval clears a calibrated similarity threshold. Each threshold was set by measurement against held-out behaviour and is recorded with its evidence. Neither was tuned to make a benchmark look good.

The obvious objection is that a large language model can simply classify the ticket. It can: on our out-of-template benchmark a zero-shot model is more accurate than our trained classifier (Section~\ref{sec:zeroshot}). But the zero-shot model offers no abstention guarantee, no calibrated gate and no cost model, and it is the gate, not the accuracy, that decides whether a wrong answer reaches a user. We report that baseline prominently because the contrast is the argument.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A calibrated two-gate escalation pipeline} whose thresholds are independently calibrated and independently re-calibratable. We report the evidence behind each threshold, including the calibration attempts that failed and the cases where the retrieval gate errs in each direction.
\item \textbf{A cross-phase finding}: the data distribution a component is fitted or calibrated on, not the method or the test applied to it, is the binding constraint. It holds for a coverage guarantee and a drift reference (calibration and reference distributions) and for a trained classifier (training distribution).
\item \textbf{Honest baselines}: a controlled ablation showing the cascade buys latency rather than accuracy, zero-shot LLM baselines from two vendors, a retrieval-sufficiency gate that fails for a reason we can name, and an audited LLM judge that fails silently.
\item \textbf{A reproducibility and audit method}: every number is emitted from a committed file into a macro, cross-platform differences are bounded by a derived rather than a fitted tolerance, and a recurring class of silent, internally consistent errors is documented case by case.
\end{enumerate}

% ===========================================================================
\section{Related Work}
% ===========================================================================
\textbf{Ticket triage.} Automated routing and escalation of IT and support tickets has been studied with classical and LLM-based classifiers~\cite{tickit,paket_ticket,redcap_llm_triage}. % TODO-VERIFY: confirm each cited work addresses ticket/request triage and routing.
These works mostly report routing accuracy. Our focus is on the abstention decision around the classifier.

\textbf{Cascades and deferral.} Confidence-based cascades defer inputs from a cheap model to an expensive one~\cite{jitkrittum_cascade}. Conformal variants replace the confidence score with a set-valued criterion~\cite{conformal_cascade}, and learning-to-defer formulations send inputs to a human expert~\cite{fanconi_defer}. % TODO-VERIFY: the characterisation of Conformal Cascade and of Fanconi et al.
We compare deferral rules at the operating coverage the live gate actually runs at. We find that averaged metrics over coverage can suggest effects the gated comparison does not support (Section~\ref{sec:method}).

\textbf{Conformal prediction under shift.} Split conformal prediction gives marginal coverage under exchangeability~\cite{vovk_alrw,angelopoulos_gentle}. Weighted conformal prediction restores it under covariate shift given the likelihood ratio~\cite{tibshirani_covshift}. Later work bounds the coverage loss beyond exchangeability~\cite{barber_beyond} and adapts online~\cite{gibbs_adaptive}. % TODO-VERIFY: which Gibbs et al. paper is intended (adaptive conformal inference vs conditional guarantees).
Our coverage measurements are an empirical instance of the gap these results describe, on text whose shift is a change of register.

\textbf{Abstention in retrieval-augmented generation.} Retrieval-augmented generation~\cite{lewis_rag} can be gated on whether the retrieved context suffices~\cite{joren_sufficient}. It can also be corrected when retrieval is poor~\cite{crag}. % TODO-VERIFY: that CRAG's mechanism is a retrieval evaluator triggering corrective actions.
We test a sufficiency rater as a second gate and report why it is not usable on our corpus.

\textbf{LLM judges.} LLM judges are increasingly used to score generations. Jung et al.~\cite{jung_trust_escalate} propose judges with guarantees of human agreement that escalate when unsure, and Jain et al.~\cite{jain_judges} study their reliability. % TODO-VERIFY: the scope of Jain et al.
Our judge agreed with human labels at a high raw rate and a negative $\kappa$, which is the failure mode these works caution against.

\textbf{Synthetic benchmarks.} LLM-generated data is increasingly used as an evaluation set~\cite{maheshwari_synthetic}. % TODO-VERIFY: Maheshwari et al.'s specific finding about synthetic benchmarks.
Our corpus is synthetic by specification, and we treat what it can and cannot measure as a result (Section~\ref{sec:setup}).

% ===========================================================================
\section{System}
\label{sec:system}
% ===========================================================================
Fig.~\ref{fig:arch} shows the pipeline. It is a sequential pipeline with agent boundaries and an HTTP surface. It is not a distributed or autonomous multi-agent system. Each stage (classify, retrieve, resolve) is an agent that declares the artifacts it depends on and decides nothing. Every routing decision lives in one orchestrator, which records a trace per stage, including stages deliberately skipped. The stages are independently addressable over HTTP. The triage endpoint still orchestrates in-process, so the measured path has no network hops.

\textbf{Classification cascade.} Tier-1 is TF-IDF with logistic regression. If its top-class probability is at least \nb{F1.gate.cascade@r2}, its label stands. Otherwise Tier-2 answers: logistic regression over frozen BGE embeddings~\cite{bge} (bge-base-en-v1.5, \nb{T18.embedding_dim} dimensions).

\textbf{Retrieval gate.} The ticket is embedded and its top-\nb{T19.rag_top_k} neighbours are retrieved from a FAISS inner-product index~\cite{faiss} over resolved tickets. If the top-1 cosine similarity is below \nb{F1.gate.rag@r2}, the ticket is escalated and no language model is called.

\textbf{Resolution.} Above the gate, Gemini (gemini-flash-lite) drafts a resolution from the retrieved tickets. Gemini never decides the category. Classification is entirely the trained models' job, and the model's only role is resolution drafting grounded in retrieved text.

The two gates are independent. The cascade threshold depends only on Tier-1's confidence, so replacing the Tier-2 embedding model does not require recalibrating it. The retrieval threshold is specific to the embedding model and must be recalibrated on any model swap. A separate offline path clusters resolved tickets by resolution text at a similarity of \nb{F1.gate.clustering@r2} and surfaces recurring clusters as automation candidates for human review.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{F1_system_architecture.pdf}
\caption{The pipeline. Two independently calibrated gates; the language model drafts only above the retrieval gate and never classifies.}
\label{fig:arch}
\end{figure}

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}
% ===========================================================================
\textbf{Origin of the corpus.} The project follows a nasscom hackathon use-case brief. The brief specified the \nb{T19.categories} categories, classification, routing, resolution suggestion, confidence-based escalation and automation flagging. It explicitly recommended a synthetic, LLM-generated dataset with title, description, category, resolution and priority fields. We followed that specification at \nb{T19.dataset_rows} rows. The synthetic corpus is therefore a followed specification, not a convenience substitute for real tickets. % TODO-VERIFY: the brief's wording and recommended dataset size, against the brief itself.

\textbf{The corpus as an object of study.} We treat the corpus as something to measure, and three measurements say what it is worth.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{The templates are the fix classes.} Resolution clustering never merges across templates, so clustering precision cannot be measured on this corpus. A pilot of the most divergent pairs found \nb{T16.pilot.false_merges} false merges. By the rule of three, that bounds the false-merge rate above by \nb{T16.pilot.rule_of_three_upper@r2}, but it cannot separate two clustering configurations. We report this as a related dataset limitation, not as an instance of the finding in Section~\ref{sec:named}.
\item \emph{Memorisation is template-level.} The corpus has \nb{T8.templates_total} templates, where a template is a (category, scenario) pair, with a median of \nb{T8.median_rows_per_template} rows each. Our in-domain calibration set touches \nb{T8.templates_touched} of them. Removing the source rows of calibration tickets therefore changes nothing. Removing whole templates would leave \nb{T8.rows_surviving_template_exclusion} of \nb{T8.dataset_rows} rows, so the calibration set cannot be de-contaminated by filtering (Table~\ref{tab:ieee_t8_contamination}).
\item \emph{Training rows buy little off-template.} A small open-weight model that never saw the corpus is indistinguishable from a classifier fitted on \nb{T19.train_rows} of its rows (Section~\ref{sec:zeroshot}).
\end{itemize}

\input{tables/ieee/T8_contamination.tex}

\textbf{Evaluation sets.} In-distribution accuracy is uninformative on template-generated data. Every model we trained scores near the ceiling on a held-out split. The in-distribution TF-IDF baseline scores \nb{T1.tfidf_baseline.in_distribution_accuracy@pct0}\%, which we treat as a warning, not a result. We therefore evaluate on three fixed, read-only sets written outside the templates:
\begin{itemize}
\item a hand-written \nb{T19.benchmark14.n}-ticket benchmark;
\item a \nb{T19.benchmark45.n}-ticket out-of-template benchmark;
\item a \nb{T19.adversarial.n}-ticket adversarial escalation set (off-topic, vague and slang tickets, each with an expected escalate-or-proceed outcome).
\end{itemize}
A separate \nb{T19.deployment175.n}-ticket deployment-distribution set, written in the benchmark's register rather than the templates', serves as a second calibration and evaluation distribution. The \nb{T19.benchmark45.n}-ticket benchmark and the deployment set were generated with Gemini. That matters for Section~\ref{sec:zeroshot}.

\textbf{Statistics.} Proportions carry a Wilson 95\% interval~\cite{wilson}. Paired comparisons on the same tickets use the exact McNemar test~\cite{mcnemar}. A difference smaller than its own noise band is reported as such and is never written as an ordered comparison. The seed is fixed throughout.

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}
% ===========================================================================
\subsection{The escalation gates and their calibration}
\label{sec:gates}
\textbf{Retrieval gate.} The threshold was chosen on a combined set of in-domain and out-of-domain tickets (Fig.~\ref{fig:ood}). At \nb{T5.gate@r2}, all \nb{T5.in_domain_proceed_at_gate} in-domain tickets proceed and \nb{T5.ood_leakage_at_gate@pct1}\% of out-of-domain tickets leak through. Lowering the threshold by two steps, to where leakage reaches \nb{T5.ood_leakage_below_gate@pct1}\%, nearly triples the leakage. The threshold also sits inside the adversarial safe range [\nb{T5.safe_range_low@r4}, \nb{T5.safe_range_high@r4}]. That range runs from the highest similarity among tickets that must escalate to the lowest among tickets that must proceed. A separate conformal novelty detector on the same similarities flags \nb{T9.adversarial_flagged} adversarial tickets and escalates \nb{T9.false_escalation_in_domain@pct1}\% of in-domain tickets at $\alpha=\nb{T7.alpha@r2}$. Its false-escalation rate is calibrated, which the hand-set threshold's is not. It is measured only and does not gate production.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{F5_ood_leakage_against_the_rag_similarity_threshold.pdf}
\caption{Out-of-domain leakage against the retrieval similarity threshold. The live gate is marked.}
\label{fig:ood}
\end{figure}

\textbf{The gate errs in both directions} (Table~\ref{tab:ieee_t17_gate_errors}). Two out-of-template benchmark tickets, \nb{T17.G021.ticket} and \nb{T17.G024.ticket}, cleared the gate at similarities of \nb{T17.G021.top_similarity@r3} and \nb{T17.G024.top_similarity@r3}. Their drafts were then labelled ungrounded by a human (Section~\ref{sec:grounded}). Ticket \nb{T17.escalated_adequate.0.ticket}, at \nb{T17.escalated_adequate.0.top_similarity@r3}, was escalated although a sufficiency rater found its retrieved context adequate. A single similarity threshold is the simplest rule that works on this corpus. It is not a claim that one scalar is sufficient.

\input{tables/ieee/T17_gate_errors.tex}

\textbf{Cascade threshold.} We made \nb{T4.calibration.attempts_total} attempts to calibrate the cascade threshold, and two were rejected.
\begin{itemize}
\item The first used the in-distribution held-out split. There, every confidence bucket is at the accuracy ceiling, so the derived threshold (\nb{T4.calibration.attempt1.threshold@r2}) looked trustworthy while telling us nothing.
\item The second used a small hand-written set. It was too sparse, and it was never committed, so we do not quote its figures.
\item The third used paraphrased tickets. At the strictest target accuracy, the derivation returns the escalate-everything sentinel (\nb{T4.sweep.threshold.target90@r4}). At the two looser targets it returns \nb{T4.sweep.threshold.target80@r2}, which is the live gate.
\end{itemize}
The in-distribution reliability numbers are a ceiling effect, not calibration. On \nb{T4.reliability.n_tickets} in-distribution tickets the observed accuracy is \nb{T4.observed_accuracy_every_bin@r1} in every bin of both tiers. The expected calibration errors (Tier-1 \nb{T4.tier1.ece@r3}, Tier-2 \nb{T4.tier2.ece@r3}) are therefore entirely the distance from confidence to that ceiling, and both tiers are under-confident there. This is why both gates were calibrated against benchmark behaviour rather than read off a predicted probability.

\subsection{Coverage transfer and the calibration distribution}
\label{sec:finding1}
We calibrate split conformal prediction for both tiers on \nb{T10.deployment.n_calibration} tickets and evaluate coverage on the out-of-template benchmark (Fig.~\ref{fig:coverage}, Table~\ref{tab:ieee_t7_t10_coverage}).

\textbf{Finding~1, in three clauses that must be read together.}
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Measured on our corpus}, split-conformal coverage transfers for the BGE representation but not the lexical one. At $\alpha=\nb{T7.alpha@r2}$ Tier-1's coverage gap is \nb{T7.tier1.coverage_gap@r3} and Tier-2's is \nb{T7.tier2.coverage_gap@r3}. The noise band is $\pm$\nb{T7.noise_band_2sd@r3} (two standard deviations over the calibration draw).
\item \emph{External replication is inconclusive.} On an external corpus that is independently generated, not real production data, a version shift left the two tiers indistinguishable (\nb{T11.7b.tier1.coverage_gap@r4} against \nb{T11.7b.tier2.coverage_gap@r4}, band $\pm$\nb{T11.7b.noise_band_2sd@r4}). A version shift is the wrong type of shift for a mechanism that is surface-vocabulary change. That corpus also has almost no representation gap to find: label accuracy is \nb{T11.7b.label_ceiling_tier1@pct1}\% for Tier-1 and \nb{T11.7b.label_ceiling_tier2@pct1}\% for Tier-2. A paraphrase shift, the right type, was blocked by its own pre-registered degeneracy rule at a domain AUC of \nb{T11.7c.tfidf_domain_auc@r4}, so no verdict was drawn. Finding~1 has been shown neither to hold nor to fail outside its original corpus.
\item \emph{Post-hoc evidence of the mechanism appears in accuracy.} Under the paraphrase shift Tier-1 lost \nb{T11.7c.accuracy.tier1_change@abs@pct1} accuracy points against Tier-2's \nb{T11.7c.accuracy.tier2_change@abs@pct1}. The difference-in-differences is \nb{T11.7c.did_point}. This is post-hoc and does not replace the blocked primary.
\end{itemize}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{F2_coverage_gap_by_representation_finding_1.pdf}
\caption{Coverage gap on the out-of-template benchmark by representation and $\alpha$, against the two-standard-deviation noise band (Finding~1, on our corpus).}
\label{fig:coverage}
\end{figure}

\input{tables/ieee/T7_T10_coverage.tex}

\textbf{The calibration distribution.} Recalibrating on the deployment-distribution set, with the same method, the same $\alpha$ and the same benchmark, moves Tier-1's gap from \nb{T10.tier1.gap_in_domain@r3} to \nb{T10.tier1.gap_deployment@r3}. Only the calibration distribution changed. Distribution matching is necessary, but it is not sufficient, since the residual stays well outside the band. For Tier-2 the payoff is set size rather than coverage.

\textbf{Weighted conformal is a partial repair, not a correction.} Reweighting calibration scores by a cross-fitted domain classifier's density ratio~\cite{tibshirani_covshift} moves Tier-1's gap by \nb{T7.weighted.tier1.delta_vs_unweighted@r3}, to \nb{T7.weighted.tier1.coverage_gap@r3}. That change is larger than the $\pm$\nb{T7.noise_band_2sd@r3} band. The residual, however, is still \nb{T7.weighted.tier1.residual_in_sd@abs@r1} standard deviations below nominal. Both readings belong together. The residuals of reweighting and of distribution matching differ by less than the band, so we make no ordered comparison between them. In BGE space the domain classifier separates the two sets with an AUC of \nb{T7.weighted.bge.domain_auc@r4}. The density ratio is ill-posed there, so that arm is blocked and its coverage figures are not a result. Separability does not imply score shift: BGE separates the sets more easily, yet it is the representation whose coverage transfers. Reweighting also has a cost, and Tier-2 pays it. In the TF-IDF-space arm, \nb{T7.weighted.tier2.tfidf.worse} Tier-2 configurations moved further from nominal, and \nb{T7.weighted.tier2.tfidf.outside_band} ended outside the band.

\subsection{The cascade buys latency, not accuracy}
\label{sec:ablation}
The obvious ablation removes the cascade by letting Tier-1 answer everything (\nb{T1.tier1only.benchmark45@frac}). The distance from there to the full pipeline, \nb{T3.repr_gap_points@r1} points, is the gap between the BGE and TF-IDF representations, not the value of cascading. The control that isolates the cascade is Tier-2 answering everything (Table~\ref{tab:ieee_t3_ablation}). Against it, the cascade is one ticket worse on each set. The difference is \nb{T3.cascade_delta.benchmark45} on the benchmark (\nb{T1.cascade.benchmark45@frac} against \nb{T1.tier2only.benchmark45@frac}, exact McNemar $p=\nb{T3.mcnemar.benchmark45@r3}$) and \nb{T3.cascade_delta.deployment175} on the deployment set (\nb{T1.cascade.deployment175@frac} against \nb{T1.tier2only.deployment175@frac}, $p=\nb{T3.mcnemar.deployment175@r3}$). What the cascade buys is latency (Table~\ref{tab:ieee_t3_latency}). Tier-2 costs \nb{T3.latency.tier2_over_tier1@r1}$\times$ Tier-1 (\nb{T3.latency.tier2_median_ms@r1} against \nb{T3.latency.tier1_median_ms@r2}\,ms median, warm, batch size one). The cascade therefore saves \nb{T3.latency.saving.benchmark45@pct0}\% of median per-ticket latency on the benchmark and \nb{T3.latency.saving.deployment175@pct0}\% on the deployment set. With the retrieval gate removed, only \nb{T3.norag.escalation_correct} adversarial tickets are handled correctly, against \nb{T3.baseline.escalation_correct} with it.

\subsection{Zero-shot LLM baselines}
\label{sec:zeroshot}
We gave two zero-shot LLMs byte-identical prompts: Gemini (gemini-flash-lite) and Qwen2.5-3B, a 3B-parameter open-weight model run locally on a laptop CPU~\cite{qwen25}. Table~\ref{tab:ieee_t1_classification} shows the results. A 3B model on a laptop CPU, with no training on this corpus, is not beaten by a classifier fitted on \nb{T19.train_rows} of its rows, and this holds across two vendors. The readings differ by pair and are not merged:
\begin{itemize}
\item Gemini scores \nb{T1.zeroshot_gemini.benchmark45@frac} (95\% CI \nb{T1.zeroshot_gemini.benchmark45@ci}) and is distinguishably better than Tier-2's \nb{T1.tier2only.benchmark45@frac} (exact McNemar $p=\nb{T1.mcnemar.gemini_vs_tier2.benchmark45@r3}$).
\item Qwen2.5-3B scores \nb{T1.zeroshot_qwen.benchmark45@frac} (95\% CI \nb{T1.zeroshot_qwen.benchmark45@ci}) and is indistinguishable from Tier-2 ($p=\nb{T1.mcnemar.qwen_vs_tier2.benchmark45@r3}$). Indistinguishable is not better.
\item Qwen2.5-3B against Gemini gives $p=\nb{T1.mcnemar.qwen_vs_gemini.benchmark45@r3}$, which is not significant.
\end{itemize}
The benchmark was generated with Gemini, so the Qwen arm is the partial control for authorship. Gemini's extra margin cannot be attributed to capability rather than authorship.

This is a zero-shot LLM against a trained classifier, which is not a like-for-like comparison. What it measures is what a template-generated training corpus is worth on out-of-template phrasing. It is not evidence that a language model outperforms the pipeline as a system. The pipeline's contribution is the calibrated escalation around the classifier, which neither zero-shot model provides. Per-category behaviour is in the supplement. Qwen never predicted Database. Infrastructure recall is \nb{T2.gemini.infrastructure.recall.benchmark45@pct0}\% for Gemini, \nb{T2.qwen.infrastructure.recall.benchmark45@pct0}\% for Qwen and \nb{T2.tier2.infrastructure.recall.benchmark45@pct0}\% for the trained classifier, which points at the tickets rather than the methods. That category's benchmark tickets had earlier needed a generation-prompt fix, because an unanchored scope had produced mislabelled tickets. % TODO-VERIFY: cite the benchmark-scope correction's details from the lab notebook in the supplement.

\subsection{Groundedness, an LLM judge, and a sufficiency gate}
\label{sec:grounded}
\textbf{Groundedness.} Every benchmark and adversarial ticket that clears the retrieval gate (\nb{T15.population.eligible} tickets) received a draft, and a human labelled each draft for whether retrieved text supports it. The labels found \nb{T14.grounded@frac} drafts grounded (95\% CI \nb{T14.grounded@ci}). The two failures share one shape. Retrieval was irrelevant, the model said so, and it then prescribed a substantive fix from general knowledge anyway.

\textbf{The LLM judge.} An LLM judge on the same rubric agreed with the human labels on \nb{T14.judge.raw_agreement} drafts, with Cohen's $\kappa=\nb{T14.judge.cohens_kappa@r3}$~\cite{cohen_kappa}. All \nb{T14.judge.n_disagreements} disagreements were the judge substituting appropriateness for support, in both directions. Used as a scaling tool, it would have reported near-universal groundedness, missed both real failures and invented a third. We treat a judge as an object of study, never as an unaudited scaling tool (Table~\ref{tab:ieee_t14_groundedness}).

\input{tables/ieee/T14_groundedness.tex}

\textbf{A sufficiency gate catches both unsupported drafts and is still not usable as a gate.} A rater that sees only the ticket and its retrieved context, never a draft, flagged \nb{T15.caught_of_ungrounded} of the ungrounded drafts. It also flagged \nb{T15.flagged_of_grounded@frac} of the grounded ones (95\% CI \nb{T15.flagged_of_grounded@ci}; Table~\ref{tab:ieee_t15_sufficiency}). As a gate it would escalate \nb{T15.escalated_of_eligible} of the tickets that currently reach the resolver to recover two bad drafts. It has no threshold to tune. The scalar gate errs in the other direction as well: ticket \nb{T17.escalated_adequate.0.ticket} was escalated although the rater found its context adequate. The near-duplicate explanation for the flags is rejected, because \nb{T14.context_distinct_fixes_2plus} of these contexts carry two or more distinct fixes. The mechanism is a measurement-target mismatch: sufficiency and groundedness are different questions. The binding limitation is the label, not the rater. The groundedness labels are an outcome proxy for draft support, so the flags are false only against that proxy. This is not an instance of the finding in Section~\ref{sec:named}.

\input{tables/ieee/T15_sufficiency.tex}

\subsection{The named finding}
\label{sec:named}
\textbf{The data distribution a component is fitted or calibrated on, not the method or the test applied to it, is the binding constraint.} It has two scoped instance classes.
\begin{itemize}
\item \emph{Calibration and reference distributions.} The first instance is coverage: recalibrating on a deployment-distribution set moved Tier-1's gap from \nb{T10.tier1.gap_in_domain@r3} to \nb{T10.tier1.gap_deployment@r3} with nothing else changed (Section~\ref{sec:finding1}). The second is drift. Legitimate deployment-register tickets flag against the in-domain drift reference at rates from \nb{T13.realistic_traffic.flag_rate.alpha0.01@r3} to \nb{T13.realistic_traffic.flag_rate.alpha0.2@r3} across the four $\alpha$ levels tested. That is between \nb{T13.realistic_traffic.ratio_to_null.min@r1} and \nb{T13.realistic_traffic.ratio_to_null.max@r1} times the per-ticket null. A monitor on that reference would alarm continuously, whatever the test, $\alpha$ or window.
\item \emph{Training distribution.} Classification is the third instance: training on the corpus does not carry to out-of-template phrasing better than no training at all (Section~\ref{sec:zeroshot}).
\end{itemize}
The template redundancy in Section~\ref{sec:setup} is a related dataset limitation, not an instance. The sufficiency result in Section~\ref{sec:grounded} is not an instance either.

We chose this wording for three reasons. \emph{Fitted or calibrated} covers the training-distribution instance without stretching the word calibration over training. \emph{The method or the test} keeps the original claim, which the drift instance needs. \emph{Component} makes the claim about each part of the pipeline rather than the system as a whole, which is how the evidence is structured.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Methodology Lessons}
\label{sec:method}
% ===========================================================================
\subsection{Ungated and averaged metrics manufacture significance}
We compared conformal deferral with the confidence incumbent. On our data the honest claim is \emph{no evidence either way on the gated axis}. None of the \nb{T12.6a.comparisons_total} comparisons showed a signal at the live gate's operating coverage (\nb{T12.6a.comparisons_with_signal} of \nb{T12.6a.comparisons_total}), and \nb{T12.6a.degenerate_configurations} configurations are degenerate there, because every rule accepts the same tickets. Area under the risk--coverage curve did return effects, but in contradictory directions across the two evaluation sets, and favouring a simpler margin baseline rather than conformal. An averaged metric covers coverages the system never runs at, so an AURC win is never a reason to promote. The same failure appeared earlier, in clustering. A valid exact binomial on which configuration won more discordant pairs would have promoted whichever one merged more. That would have inverted the precision-over-recall rule the gate exists to enforce, and it would have done so on zero evidence about correctness. We replaced that rule before any label was collected.

\subsection{A pre-registered rule is not revised after the fact}
The paraphrase-shift experiment copied its degeneracy rule from the weighted-conformal experiment, where the rule guarded a density-ratio estimate. The paraphrase design computes no density ratio. It uses the domain AUC only as a manipulation check, where a value near one means the manipulation was strong. That critique is sound, and we still did not unblock the result, because revising a pre-registered rule after seeing results is exactly what the discipline exists to prevent. We record it as a specification error. A counter-reading is recorded too: a rewrite that a classifier identifies with near-certainty may be a different corpus rather than a shifted one. The lesson is that a degeneracy rule must be justified by what the specific design estimates, never copied across designs.

\subsection{A recurring class of silent errors}
Nine times, a value or artifact was wrong for its context, stayed internally consistent, and produced a wrong result without raising an error:
\begin{enumerate}
\item a stale embedding cache during the embedding-model swap;
\item a gate script that kept its own copies of the old model's constants;
\item a batch script that encoded with one model against another model's index;
\item an ablation that measured the entire pre-swap pipeline, which reached published results;
\item an eligibility test on the wrong status enum, which would have drafted for tickets production never sends to the resolver;
\item a template grouping key missing its category component, which reached published results;
\item a container ignore rule that did not match nested paths, so the image was built from a developer's cached embeddings;
\item provenance hashes of line-ending-dependent working-tree bytes, which reported every source as changed on another platform;
\item found while writing this paper: an ablation table counting adversarial tickets that \emph{escalated} as tickets \emph{decided correctly}, beside an arm counted by correctness.
\end{enumerate}
The shape generalises beyond model swaps, to routing tests, grouping keys, packaging rules and hashes. Most were caught by a second, independent derivation of a count. The supplement gives each in full.

\subsection{Correcting published numbers}
We correct in place rather than soften.
\begin{itemize}
\item The ablation had been measuring the pre-swap pipeline. Re-run, the baseline is \nb{T1.cascade.benchmark45@pct1}\%, and the gap it had been attributed to belongs to representation, not cascading (Section~\ref{sec:ablation}).
\item The template-contamination diagnostic grouped by scenario alone and merged all categories. It now reads \nb{T8.templates_total} templates (Section~\ref{sec:setup}), and its conclusion survived because the coverage measurement excludes by row, not by template.
\item The TF-IDF baseline's figure on the hand-written benchmark did not reproduce when given a result writer. It is \nb{T1.tfidf_baseline.benchmark14}, and three independent derivations agree.
\item The drift ratio we had quoted, and the gate-distance headroom behind our parity tolerance, were both recomputed from committed files for this paper, and we quote the recomputed values.
\end{itemize}

% ===========================================================================
\section{Reproducibility}
\label{sec:repro}
% ===========================================================================
\textbf{Numbers from committed files.} Every number in this paper is emitted by one build script from a committed result file into a macro. A test fails if any emitted value, table or figure datum moves. A lint fails if a number is typed into the build script's emit calls or into this document. We adopted the rule after two domain AUCs, computed interactively and quoted at a review gate, did not reproduce when respecified.

\textbf{Container and CI.} A digest-pinned container builds its own artifacts in documented order and refuses to build if a pre-built artifact reaches its context. Its health endpoint serves the configuration fingerprint, which a committed verifier compares with the checkout's. Two CI workflows run the suite, the adversarial gate and the ablation baseline; neither can spend API quota.

\textbf{Decisions reproduce; embedding floats do not} (Table~\ref{tab:ieee_t18_platform}). Category, tier, escalation and neighbour count are compared exactly on all \nb{T18.golden_tickets} golden tickets. That comparison \nb{T18.runner_07136ec.golden_parity.outcome} on a CI runner. Similarities are float32 inner products accumulated in an order set by the BLAS kernel and SIMD width. On one ticket, the recorded similarity differed from our reference by \nb{T18.container_8b.adv_08.rag_similarity.abs_delta@sci2} in a local container and by \nb{T18.runner_91a5b38.adv_08.rag_similarity.abs_delta@sci2} on a CI runner. We computed these differences from raw values recorded once on those platforms; they are not re-derivable on our machine. Parity is therefore asserted with a derived bound: $\gamma_n = nu/(1-nu) = \nb{T18.gamma_n@sci2}$ for $n=\nb{T18.embedding_dim}$ at single-precision unit roundoff~\cite{higham}. The bound covers the inner product only; it does not model the encoder's own cross-platform difference. A test fails if any golden value sits within its tolerance of the gate it feeds. The closest golden similarity is \nb{T18.headroom.similarity_distance@sci2} from the gate, \nb{T18.headroom.similarity_ratio@r2}$\times$ the tolerance, which is thin, and we report it rather than engineer it away.

\input{tables/ieee/T18_platform.tex}

\textbf{The lexical vocabulary was not determined by the data.} A vectorizer capped at \nb{T18.ties.full4000.max_features} features keeps the most frequent terms with an unstable sort. On the full corpus \nb{T18.ties.full4000.above_cut} terms sit above the cut and \nb{T18.ties.full4000.tied_at_cut} tie for the remaining \nb{T18.ties.full4000.slots_for_tied} slots. That is \nb{T18.ties.full4000.share@pct1}\% of the features chosen by the sort's tie-break, and the sort differs by CPU. A CI runner therefore produced a Tier-1 confidence \nb{T18.runner_91a5b38.adv_08.tier1_confidence.abs_delta@sci2} away from ours on an unchanged model. We now commit the vocabulary as an artifact and fit against it. No decision moved. Four experiment fits keep the same configuration deliberately, because refitting them would move published numbers. On the training split their tie is \nb{T18.ties.split3200.slots_for_tied} of \nb{T18.ties.split3200.max_features} features, so their figures reproduce on our platform and may differ slightly on another.

\textbf{Fine-tuning variance.} Two fine-tuning runs of the same DistilBERT configuration agree exactly on the hand-written benchmark (\nb{T1.distilbert.benchmark14}). On the out-of-template benchmark they give \nb{T1.distilbert.benchmark45} and \nb{T1.distilbert.reference.benchmark45}, so CPU fine-tuning does not reproduce better than the difference between those two runs on that axis. We make no ordered comparison between them.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Limitations}
% ===========================================================================
\textbf{Synthetic corpus.} All of our training data and most of our evaluation data are synthetic. The external corpus tests whether findings survive a different generator, not whether they survive reality.

\textbf{Small evaluation sets, and accumulating selection risk.} At \nb{T19.benchmark45.n} tickets a single ticket moves accuracy visibly, and many of our comparisons are indistinguishable for that reason alone. The same benchmark has informed many decisions across the project, so its independence from our design choices erodes with each use.

\textbf{Gemini authored much of the evaluation data.} The out-of-template benchmark and the deployment set were generated with the same model family used for resolution drafting and for one zero-shot arm.

\textbf{The adversarial gate is a regression test, not validation.} Passing all \nb{T19.adversarial.n} adversarial tickets shows that behaviour did not change. It does not show that the gate generalises.

\textbf{Unaudited external labels.} The external corpus's labels were assigned by its generator and were not audited. Label accuracy there is at most \nb{T11.7b.label_ceiling_tier2@pct1}\%.

\textbf{No production deployment.} No real ticket stream has passed through the system. The drift monitor has no deployment reference, and the escalation rate we report is a property of generated tickets, not of production traffic.

% ===========================================================================
\section{Conclusion and Future Work}
% ===========================================================================
A triage pipeline's value lies in knowing when not to answer. We built two calibrated escalation gates, measured them honestly, and found that the distribution each component was fitted or calibrated on bounded what it could achieve, whatever the method. Three directions follow. The first is a set-size hypothesis: coverage may be buffered by large prediction sets, so a representation contrast may need small sets before it shows. The second is a drift reference built from deployment-register traffic. The third, and the one the others depend on, is evaluation on real ticket data.
